paras: The attempted lynching of Alexander Goldensen was a mob attack on a San Francisco jail in November 1886, in which a crowd tried to seize and lynch a young man held for shooting a 14-year-old schoolgirl, Mamie Kelly. The police drove the mob off, and reports of his execution counted two such attempts, both stopped by police. Goldensen was tried, convicted and hanged legally on September 14, 1888, an execution that the wire report said had excited more interest on the Pacific coast than any since the days of the vigilance committee.

Goldensen, whose name was also printed as Goldenson, was said to have come from Russia and to have been studying art; the papers gave his age at the time of the crime as 18 or 19. According to a May 1888 San Francisco dispatch, he had escorted Mamie Kelly to several entertainments until her mother forbade her to go with him. On the afternoon of November 10, 1886, as she walked home from school toward her grandmother's house on Hayes street, he met her at the corner of Polk and McAllister streets and shot her dead with a pistol.

A crowd chased Goldensen as he fled, and he found refuge in the police station. On the following night, the same dispatch reported, "a mob of several thousand" tried to break into the County Jail and lynch him, but it "had no leader," and police were summoned and drove the crowd away. The wire report of the hanging said that his crime "came near causing a riot" and that two attempts were made to lynch him by assaulting the jail, which it called the city jail, with police preventing serious disorder each time. A special dispatch to the St. Paul Globe placed both attempts within the two years after the murder; no paper describes the second attempt or reports injuries.

No arrests of mob members are reported in the coverage. Goldensen was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to hang; he pleaded hereditary insanity, and his appeal argued he had not been given time to gather evidence from Russia, but the state Supreme Court affirmed the sentence in May 1888. Governor Waterman declined clemency, and the Sacramento Record-Union said the decision would "meet with public approval."

Crowds sought tickets to the execution, for which 450 invitations were issued. Goldensen was hanged in the jail a few minutes after noon on September 14, 1888. Afterward his parents sued Coroner Stanton for the return of his brain, which the coroner had kept to refute any later claim of insanity.

Only white papers covered the case, and they told it as the story of a murderer's execution rather than of a mob. The September 14 wire ran the same day in papers from Indianapolis and New York to Savannah and Unionville, Nevada, and in reprints over the following week in Washington, Richmond, Wheeling, Atlanta, Kansas and Louisiana. In that wire, the lynching attempts took up a single sentence, set beside "the popular feeling against the young murderer" and his last night of "drinking, card playing and blasphemy."

Headlines aimed their scorn at Goldensen, not at the mob: the New York Sun ran "A California Wretch Hanged," the Savannah Morning News "Courted a Trip to Sheol," and the Springfield Daily Republic "The World to be Rid of One Rascal." The Elko Daily Independent wrote that the mob that chased him would, had it caught him, "have saved the State the expense of a trial and the Sheriff the trouble of hanging him."

Accounts differ on details: most give the girl's name as Mamie Kelly, aged 14, while one wire copy has "Mattie" and the Springfield dispatch says she was fifteen. The Springfield dispatch, the only account of the attempt with detail, names the County Jail, where the wire says the city jail, and it is not clear whether the street pursuit was one of the wire's two attempts.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Alexander Goldensen
bases: A crowd chased Goldensen after the shooting and a mob tried to break into the jail to lynch him, which the wire reports count as two ineffectual lynching attempts (A1, A5, A10).

A mob of 'several thousand' tried to take Goldensen from jail and lynch him for the shooting of Mamie Kelly, but the police drove it off (A1, A10); he was hanged legally by the sheriff on Sept. 14, 1888 after a trial and appeals (A5, A1), so no one was killed by the mob.

The May 1888 Springfield report (A1), the Associated Press-style wire of Sept. 14 (A5-A9), the St. Paul Globe special (A10) and the Elko Daily Independent (A16) all report mob action against Goldensen after the shooting, though only A1 gives any detail.

San Francisco: the shooting at the corner of Polk and McAllister streets; the attempted lynching at the jail ('County Jail' in A1, 'city jail' in the wire).
Alexander Goldensen (also spelled Goldenson), target of the lynching attempts; not harmed by the mob. No paper gives his race; A1 says he came from Russia and was studying art.
Shooting and killing Mamie (or Mattie) Kelly, a 14-year-old schoolgirl (15 in A1), reportedly after she rejected his attentions; he was later convicted of first-degree murder.
A crowd that pursued him to the police station, and a mob that tried to break into the jail; no leader.
Goldensen was hanged legally in the jail a few minutes after noon on Sept. 14, 1888.
